cards.back: Replication copies the same data to more machines; sharding splits the data so each machine holds only part. Each shard is usually its own replicated group.
A bigger machine, read replicas, a cache, archiving old data, and splitting unrelated tables into separate databases.
Vertical splits by columns or features (separate tables or databases); horizontal sharding splits one table's rows across machines.
Contiguous key ranges: great for range scans, but new data all lands on the last range and makes it hot.
hash(key) picks the shard: even load, but range queries must ask every shard.
A lookup table maps keys or tenants to shards, so one big tenant can be moved on its own. Cache the directory; it's a critical dependency.
Many evenly spread values, matches the main access pattern so most queries hit one shard, and keeps things that change together on one shard.
Going from 4 to 5 shards changes the answer for about 80% of keys, so almost all data moves or every cache entry misses.
Nodes and keys hash onto a ring and a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node takes only about 1/N of the keys.
Each physical node gets 100 to 200 points on the ring to even out the load.
Create something like 1,024 logical shards up front and place many on each machine, so growth moves whole shards instead of re-splitting keys.
A query without the shard key goes to every shard and merges results, getting slower as shards grow. Keep a secondary index keyed the other way instead.

quiz.q: A chat app shards messages. Which shard key keeps most queries on one shard?
quiz.why: Queries are scoped to a conversation, so its messages and transactions stay local.

quiz.q: You shard orders by date range and the newest shard is overloaded. Why?
choices: All new writes land on the last range
quiz.why: Range sharding by time sends every new write to one shard.

quiz.q: Using hash(key) % N, you add a fifth cache node and the database is flooded. Why?
choices: About 80% of keys now map to a different node, so most lookups miss
quiz.why: Modulo hashing reshuffles almost everything; consistent hashing moves only about 1/N.

quiz.q: With consistent hashing and only one point per node, load is very uneven. What fixes it?
choices: Virtual nodes: many points per physical node
quiz.why: Many ring points per node even out each node's share.

quiz.q: Users are sharded by user_id, but login looks users up by email. What keeps that fast?
choices: Store every user on every shard
quiz.why: A secondary index keyed the other way avoids asking every shard.

quiz.q: One huge tenant overwhelms its hash shard. Which strategy lets you move just that tenant?
quiz.why: A directory maps each tenant to a shard, so one can be moved on its own.

quiz.q: You expect to grow from 16 to 64 machines. How do you avoid re-splitting keys later?
choices: Start with 16 shards and rehash later
Create many logical shards up front and move whole shards
quiz.why: Moving logical shards between machines avoids rehashing keys.
